section.title: Firstfruits and Tithes
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the law section with worship: bringing the first and best of the harvest with a recited confession of Israel's whole redemption story, giving the third-year tithe to the vulnerable, and a covenant renewal formula, the LORD as Israel's God, Israel as His treasured people, sealing everything that has come before.
section.thesis: Having given Israel its statutes, the LORD now teaches Israel how to worship in response: bringing firstfruits with a recited history of grace, from a wandering Aramean, to slavery, to redemption, to the land, sharing the tithe with the vulnerable, and confessing on this day that the LORD is Israel's God and Israel is His treasured possession.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the offering of firstfruits with its recited confession of Israel's whole story of grace; the third-year tithe for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow with its declaration of obedience; and the covenant's mutual, this-day confession, the LORD as Israel's God, Israel as His treasured people.

verses.text: When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, and you take possession of it and settle in it,

you are to take some of the {{bikkurim|firstfruits}} of all your produce from the soil of the land that the LORD your God is giving you and put them in a basket. Then go to the place the LORD your God will choose as a dwelling for His Name,
to the priest who is serving at that time, and say to him, "I declare today to the LORD your God that I have entered the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us."
Then the priest shall take the basket from your hands and place it before the altar of the LORD your God,
and you are to declare before the LORD your God, "My father was a {{oved|wandering}} Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation, mighty and numerous.
But the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor.
So we called out to the LORD, the God of our fathers; and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression.
Then the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, signs, and wonders.
And He brought us to this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.
And now, behold, I have brought the firstfruits of the land that You, O LORD, have given me." Then you are to place the basket before the LORD your God and bow down before Him.
So you shall rejoice, you, the Levite, and the foreigner dwelling among you, in all the good things the LORD your God has given to you and your household.

When you have finished laying aside a tenth of all your produce in the third year, the year of the tithe, you are to give it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat and be filled within your gates.

Then you shall declare in the presence of the LORD your God, "I have removed from my house the sacred portion and have given it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all the commandments You have given me. I have not transgressed or forgotten Your commandments.

I have not eaten any of the sacred portion while in mourning, or removed any of it while unclean, or offered any of it for the dead. I have obeyed the LORD my God; I have done everything You commanded me.
Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel and the land You have given us as You swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey."

units.label: A covenant confessed, this day
units.note: the LORD your God, His treasured people

verses.text: The LORD your God commands you this day to follow these statutes and ordinances. You must be careful to follow them with all your heart and with all your soul.
Today you have proclaimed that the LORD is your God and that you will walk in His ways, keep His statutes and commandments and ordinances, and listen to His voice.
And today the LORD has proclaimed that you are His people and {{segullah|treasured possession}} as He promised, that you are to keep all His commandments,
that He will set you high in praise and name and honor above all the nations He has made, and that you will be a holy people to the LORD your God, as He has promised.

oved.gloss: Wandering, perishing, about to be lost. The declaration 'my father was a wandering Aramean' recalls Jacob's precarious, landless beginnings, grounding Israel's worship in the memory of God's rescue of the helpless.

bikkurim.gloss: Firstfruits, the first and best of the harvest, offered in gratitude and trust before the rest of the produce is used or enjoyed.

segullah.gloss: Treasured possession, a king's own private treasure. Used of Israel as God's own particular, cherished people, distinct from His general ownership of all creation, and later applied to the church, 1 Peter 2:9.

basic.context: As the specific law code closes, Moses teaches Israel a liturgy: bringing the first and best of every harvest to the place the LORD chooses, and reciting there the whole story of God's grace, from Jacob's precarious wandering, through slavery in Egypt, to rescue and the gift of the land. Every third year the tithe goes instead to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, with its own spoken declaration of obedience. The chapter closes with a mutual confession: the LORD is Israel's God, and Israel is His treasured people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historically specific liturgy for worship in the land God was giving Israel, tied to its own agricultural calendar and its own redemption from Egypt; the deeper pattern, worship as grateful recitation of God's saving acts rather than bare ritual, and generosity toward the vulnerable as an act of obedience, remains for God's people in every era.
basic.originalLanguages: The confession recalls Jacob as an oved, a wandering, nearly perishing, Aramean, deliberately humbling Israel's origin story before recounting the LORD's rescue. The offering itself is bikkurim, firstfruits, the first and best given in trust before the rest is used. And Israel is called God's segullah, treasured possession, a king's own private treasure, not merely one nation among many He happens to own.
basic.typology: The recited confession, 'my father was a wandering Aramean,' models the pattern of gospel proclamation itself: naming helplessness honestly, then recounting God's saving action in history, the very shape of apostolic preaching in Acts.
basic.christ: Israel's identity as God's segullah, treasured possession, is picked up directly in 1 Peter 2:9, where the church, Jew and Gentile united in Christ, is called 'a chosen people... God's own possession,' the pattern set here fulfilled and widened in the people gathered around Jesus.
basic.god: God delights to be recounted, not merely believed in silently: Israel's worship is built around retelling exactly what He has done, and His generosity toward Israel becomes the model for Israel's own generosity toward the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 2:9 applies 'God's own possession' directly to the church. Exodus 19:5 first calls Israel God's treasured possession at Sinai. Titus 2:14 says Christ redeemed a people 'of His own, eager to do good works.' Nehemiah 9 offers a later, similar historical recitation of God's saving acts.
basic.oneStory: Israel's worship rehearses the whole story of grace so far, from wandering exile to promised land, and calls Israel God's own treasured people, a pattern and a title the New Testament takes up to describe the church, gathered from every nation through Christ, as God's treasured possession.

context.literary:
This chapter forms a deliberate three part liturgy that closes the legal core of Deuteronomy with worship rather than one more statute, a firstfruits ritual with its spoken confession, verses 1 to 11, the third year tithe declaration, verses 12 to 15, and a covenant ratification formula, verses 16 to 19. Each section is built around speech Israel must actually say aloud, "you are to declare," verses 3, 5, and 13, so the whole chapter functions less as instruction about worship and more as a script for it.

The firstfruits confession, verses 5 to 10, is itself a tightly compressed history of Israel in six clauses, humble origin, descent to Egypt, affliction, a cry for help, rescue, and gift of land. It moves from third person, "my father," to first person plural, "we," to first person singular, "I," tracking Israel's story from ancestral memory to the worshiper's own present act of thanksgiving, so each individual Israelite personally inhabits the nation's whole history every time the basket is brought.

The chapter's closing unit, verses 16 to 19, is built as a matched pair of proclamations, "today you have proclaimed... today the LORD has proclaimed," the only place in Deuteronomy where covenant commitment is described as mutual and simultaneous rather than simply commanded by God and accepted by Israel. This mutuality forms a fitting hinge before the blessings and curses that follow, since chapter 26 establishes the relationship whose terms chapters 27 and 28 will spell out in full.
context.historical:
The firstfruits basket, brought "to the place the LORD your God will choose," verse 2, presumes the central sanctuary Deuteronomy has already established, later Shiloh and then Jerusalem, where a priest received the offering directly from the worshiper's hands. Bringing produce still fresh from the field before using any of it themselves tied the whole nation's worship to its actual agricultural calendar, so gratitude was not an abstract feeling but something rehearsed every harvest season.

The confession's description of Jacob as an oved Aramean recalls his years as a dependent laborer under Laban in Paddan-aram, Genesis 29 to 31, a period the patriarch himself later described as insecure and precarious, working for another man's wages far from any land of his own. That a nation now settled and prosperous in Canaan was required to speak this humbling ancestry aloud, rather than simply recount its later triumphs, kept Israel's worship rooted in the memory of genuine helplessness rather than in any sense of inherited status.

The third year tithe answered a real structural gap in Israelite society. The Levites held no tribal land allotment, Deuteronomy 14:27 and 29, and foreigners, orphans, and widows likewise lacked the ordinary means of self support that land and family gave most Israelites, so a recurring, locally stored provision every third year functioned as a built in social safety net rather than occasional charity left to individual generosity.

The closing covenant formula, verses 16 to 19, uses treaty language recognizable across the ancient Near East, mutual declarations binding both parties, though here reshaped so Israel's obligation and the LORD's promise are spoken in the same breath rather than negotiated between equals.
context.canonical:
The title "treasured possession," segullah, verse 18, is not new here. The LORD first offers it to Israel at Sinai, conditioned on obedience, Exodus 19:5, and Deuteronomy repeats it earlier as an already settled fact, Deuteronomy 7:6 and 14:2, so by chapter 26 the title functions as summary and seal rather than fresh announcement. The New Testament then transfers the same word directly onto the church, "a people for God's own possession," 1 Peter 2:9, and Paul uses nearly identical language for those Christ "redeemed... to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds," Titus 2:14, extending a title first spoken over ethnic Israel to a people gathered from every nation through the Messiah.

The firstfruits confession itself becomes a template. Centuries later, the Levites lead all Israel in a strikingly similar recitation after the exile, tracing the same movement from the call of Abraham through slavery, deliverance, and gift of land, Nehemiah 9:6 to 8, showing later generations returned instinctively to this pattern of worship as rehearsed history whenever the nation needed to remember who it was and whose it was.

Joshua's own farewell address adopts the identical historical recital form, beginning "long ago your fathers... lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods," Joshua 24:2 to 4, before calling Israel to renewed covenant loyalty, confirming that Deuteronomy 26's confession set a lasting pattern for how Israel would be taught to remember its own story at moments of covenant renewal.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants a settled, prosperous Israel never to worship as though its blessings were self made. By scripting an actual confession the worshiper must speak aloud, rather than leaving gratitude to private feeling, he ties every harvest to the specific, historical acts of a specific God, not to vague thankfulness for good fortune. He wants each generation, however many years removed from the exodus, to say "my father was a wandering Aramean" as though it happened to them personally, collapsing the distance between the nation's past and any individual worshiper's present moment.

He also wants generosity toward the powerless built into Israel's regular worship calendar rather than left to occasional impulse, timing a structured provision for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow to coincide with the very rhythm of firstfruits worship, so gratitude to God and generosity to the vulnerable are taught as one movement, not two separate duties.

Finally, by closing the whole legal section with mutual proclamation, "today you have proclaimed... today the LORD has proclaimed," Moses wants Israel to feel the weight of a relationship freely entered rather than merely imposed, a covenant Israel itself speaks into being with its own mouth on the plains of Moab before it ever crosses the Jordan.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific liturgical mechanics, bringing a basket to one central sanctuary, the priest physically taking it from the worshiper's hands, the exact wording of the spoken confession, describe Israel's own old covenant worship tied to a land, a temple, and an agricultural calendar the church does not share. No New Testament instruction tells believers to recite this confession or to observe a third year tithe cycle.

What does carry forward is the pattern beneath the mechanics, worship that rehearses concretely what God has actually done rather than staying at the level of general praise, and generosity toward the vulnerable treated as integral to worship rather than an optional add on to it. Paul's instruction that giving should be planned and regular rather than reluctant, 2 Corinthians 9:7, echoes the same rhythm this chapter sets up, gratitude expressed on a schedule, not only when it happens to occur to someone. The title "treasured possession" likewise moves from description of ethnic Israel to a status every believer in Christ now shares, 1 Peter 2:9, showing a covenant identity once spoken only over one nation now true of the whole church.

debates.question: Does the third year tithe of verses 12-15 replace or supplement the regular annual tithe described elsewhere in Deuteronomy?

views.label: A distinct, additional welfare tithe every third year
views.case: Many interpreters see this as a separate tithe, beyond the annual tithe of chapter 14, specifically directed to the poor and vulnerable rather than consumed at the central sanctuary, forming a structured, recurring welfare provision.

views.label: The same tithe redirected in its third year cycle
views.case: Others read this as the same tithe of chapter 14, which in most years was eaten by the family at the sanctuary, being redirected every third year specifically to local storage for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text establishes a recurring, structured provision for the vulnerable built into Israel's worship calendar, not a matter of occasional charity alone.

debates.question: Does "my father was a wandering Aramean," verse 5, describe Jacob's own precarious state, or Laban's hostility toward him?

views.label: Jacob himself as homeless and near destitute
views.case: Most English translations, including the BSB, render oved as "wandering," describing Jacob's own condition, a man without land of his own who served another man's household for years in Paddan-aram, Genesis 29 to 31, before going down into Egypt still "few in number," verse 5.

views.label: An Aramean, Laban, who tried to destroy Jacob
views.case: The Hebrew word order can also be read as "an Aramean sought to destroy my father," taking Aram as the subject rather than the description of the father, a reading with a long history in Jewish liturgy, where the Passover Haggadah recites this verse of Laban's hostility toward Jacob, Genesis 31:23 to 29, rather than of Jacob's own homelessness.

debates.bearing: Either reading keeps the confession's whole point intact, Israel's ancestor arrived at greatness only because God rescued him from real danger, whether the danger was landless poverty or a kinsman's active hostility, so the worshiper's gratitude rests on rescue either way.

study.originalLanguages:
The confession's very first word about Israel's ancestor, oved, is genuinely double edged. Its root can mean simply "wandering" or "lost," matching most English translations' "my father was a wandering Aramean," but the same root elsewhere means "to perish" or "be destroyed," close enough in sense that Jewish tradition has long read the clause instead as "an Aramean sought to destroy my father," pointing at Laban's hostility toward Jacob rather than Jacob's own homelessness. Either way, the confession opens by refusing Israel any dignity of origin, whichever reading is right, the ancestor of the whole nation began in danger, not strength.

The offering itself is bikkurim, verse 2, built from a root meaning "first" or "firstborn," the same family of words used for a firstborn son or animal, so giving God the first produce of the land carries the same weight as consecrating a firstborn child, a portion set apart before the rest is claimed for ordinary use.

Three times the chapter uses the verb "declare," higgid, verses 3, 5, and 13, a strong verb of testimony rather than casual speech, the same verb used when a witness reports what he has personally seen, underlining that Israel's confession is not liturgy recited by rote but sworn testimony to events the speaker claims as real.

The closing title segullah, "treasured possession," verse 18, is a term borrowed from royal administration, describing a king's personal, movable wealth, distinct from state property generally, the kind of treasure a king kept for himself rather than held in trust for the kingdom at large. Applying this word to Israel says God does not merely rule Israel as territory among His wider dominion; He claims the nation as personally and particularly His own, the way a king claims his own private treasury.

The basket that carries the offering, tene, verse 2, is a plain, everyday container, not a special ritual vessel reserved for the sanctuary, a small detail suggesting the offering itself belongs to ordinary agricultural life brought directly into worship rather than to anything manufactured or set apart beforehand.

The mutual proclamation of verses 17 and 18 uses a rare, causative form of the ordinary verb "to say," found in this exact construction only in these two verses of the Hebrew Bible, "you have caused the LORD to say" and "the LORD has caused you to say," by which the text itself grammatically pictures each party as bringing the other's declaration into being, a linguistic mirror of the covenant's own mutuality.

typology.fulfillment: The confession's shape, naming humble or desperate beginnings honestly before recounting God's saving acts in history, becomes the basic pattern of apostolic preaching. Peter's sermon at Pentecost and Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin both retell Israel's history from the patriarchs through slavery to deliverance before arriving at their real subject, Christ, Acts 2:14-36 and Acts 7:2-53. The gospel is proclaimed the same way firstfruits were confessed, as a true story rehearsed aloud, not a private feeling described. The type is a pattern of proclamation rather than a foreshadowing of a single event, and it never claims Christ as its direct fulfillment, only as the pattern's clearest New Testament use.

typology.type: Israel named the LORD's treasured possession, Deuteronomy 26:18
typology.fulfillment: The exact title given here is transferred without qualification onto the church in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike gathered into "a people for God's own possession," 1 Peter 2:9, and Paul describes believers as those Christ "redeemed... to purify for Himself a people for His own possession," Titus 2:14. What was once Israel's national title by covenant becomes the church's identity by faith in the Messiah, widening a title once spoken over one ethnic nation into one spoken over every believer united to Christ, the fulfillment escalating the promise from a nation to a people drawn "from every nation, tribe, and tongue," Revelation 7:9.

Giving God the first and best of the harvest before using any of it anticipates Paul's description of Christ Himself as "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," 1 Corinthians 15:20, the first installment of the resurrection harvest still to come. Just as Israel's firstfruits basket guaranteed the rest of the crop was truly theirs to enjoy, Christ's own resurrection guarantees the full resurrection of everyone joined to Him. The correspondence is one of principle rather than a directly stated fulfillment, since Paul's phrase draws on the broader biblical image of firstfruits as a pledge rather than quoting this specific chapter.

typology.type: The third year tithe for the vulnerable, Deuteronomy 26:12-15
typology.fulfillment: Structured, recurring provision for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow anticipates the New Testament pattern of the church's own care for "orphans and widows in their distress," James 1:27, and Paul's collection for the Jerusalem poor, planned in advance and gathered on a set schedule, 1 Corinthians 16:1-2. The type is one of principle, not of a single fulfilled event, since the New Testament never treats this tithe as a shadow finally realized in one act, only as an abiding pattern of structured generosity that the church inherits and continues in its own way.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first through its central title. Israel is called God's segullah, treasured possession, verse 18, a title first offered conditionally at Sinai, Exodus 19:5, and now confirmed as settled fact. The New Testament lifts this exact title off ethnic Israel and places it, without qualification, on the church gathered in Christ, "a people for God's own possession," 1 Peter 2:9, and Paul describes believers as those Christ "redeemed... to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds," Titus 2:14. A title once spoken over one nation at one mountain now describes everyone united to Jesus by faith, drawn from every nation rather than one.

It leads to Christ through the confession's own pattern. "My father was a wandering Aramean" names humble, even perilous beginnings honestly before turning to what God has done, exactly the shape apostolic preaching takes when Peter and Stephen retell Israel's history before arriving at the crucified and risen Christ, Acts 2:14-36 and 7:2-53. The gospel is announced the way firstfruits were confessed, true history spoken aloud, not vague sentiment.

It leads to Christ through the offering's own logic. Bringing the first and best of the harvest before touching the rest of it, trusting there is more to come, anticipates Paul's description of the risen Christ as "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," 1 Corinthians 15:20, the first installment of a resurrection harvest guaranteed to follow. Israel's basket said, in effect, the rest belongs to us because God has already given us this; Christ's resurrection says the same thing about every believer's future.

Finally, the mutual proclamation that closes the chapter, "today you have proclaimed... today the LORD has proclaimed," anticipates a covenant no longer built on Israel's own performance but sealed in Christ's blood, "this cup is the new covenant in My blood," Luke 22:20, where God's declaration over His people rests entirely on what His Son has done rather than on a confession Israel must first get right.
study.god:
God, in this chapter, delights to be recounted rather than merely believed in the abstract. He scripts an actual speech for Israel to say, insisting that worship name specific events, a wandering ancestor, slavery, a cry heard, a rescue accomplished, a land given, rather than settling for a vague thankfulness that could describe any god or none. He wants to be known by what He has actually done, not praised in generalities.

He is a God who identifies with beginnings that are anything but impressive. The confession He scripts opens with weakness, near destitution or active danger, depending how oved is read, refusing to let Israel's later prosperity erase the memory of how little it once had. A God secure enough in His own greatness lets His people's worship start with their own smallness.

He binds His own generosity to Israel's, in both directions. Israel gives Him firstfruits because He gave the land; Israel then gives to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow because He gave to Israel, so gratitude toward God and generosity toward the powerless are one movement flowing from a single source, not two separate obligations competing for attention.

He is a covenant partner who binds Himself as much as He binds Israel. The chapter's closing formula does not read as command answered by compliance; it reads as two declarations spoken in the same breath, "today you have proclaimed... today the LORD has proclaimed," as though God places His own word on the table alongside Israel's, staking His name on the relationship exactly as He asks Israel to stake its obedience.

And He is a God who intends His people's distinction among the nations to serve them, not merely flatter them, promising to set Israel "high in praise and name and honor above all the nations," verse 19, language that later shapes how Israel understands its calling to be a light drawing others toward the God who chose it, rather than a status to be hoarded for itself.

crossReferences.note: Peter applies "a people for God's own possession" directly to the church, Jew and Gentile united in Christ, taking the very title given to Israel here and declaring it fulfilled in those called out of darkness into God's marvelous light.

The LORD first offers Israel the title treasured possession at Sinai, conditioned on obedience and covenant keeping, and Deuteronomy 26:18 repeats the same word as an accomplished fact on the plains of Moab.

Paul describes Christ as redeeming a people "for His own possession, zealous for good deeds," echoing this chapter's segullah and grounding the church's identity in what Christ has done rather than in national descent.

The Levites lead a returned, chastened Israel through a strikingly similar recitation of its history, from Abraham's call through the exodus, showing later generations returned instinctively to this pattern of confession at moments of covenant renewal.

Joshua's farewell address opens with the same historical recital form, "long ago your fathers... lived beyond the Euphrates," before calling Israel to renewed covenant loyalty, confirming this chapter set a lasting shape for Israel's corporate memory.

Stephen's defense before the Sanhedrin retells Israel's history from Abraham through the exodus before arriving at its true point, the crucified and risen Christ, following the same pattern of confession this chapter scripts for the firstfruits worshiper.

Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," an image drawn from the broader biblical picture of firstfruits as a pledge guaranteeing the rest of the harvest still to come for all who trust Him.

Describes the same third year tithe cycle for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, whether as the same tithe redirected or a distinct provision, tying chapter 26's declaration to an established, recurring practice.

Commands leaving gleanings in field, olive grove, and vineyard for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, the same three vulnerable groups named in the third year tithe, weaving care for them into more than one part of Israel's economy.

Defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their distress, echoing the same vulnerable pair this chapter names, and showing the New Testament carries forward Israel's structured concern as a mark of genuine faith.

study.oneStory:
This chapter closes Israel's law with worship because the whole story the law serves is, at bottom, a story of rescue answered by gratitude. From creation's abundance, through the fall's fracture, God has been at work rescuing a helpless people, and this chapter teaches Israel to say so out loud every single harvest, "my father was a wandering Aramean," a confession that could just as easily open the story of anyone in Christ, rescued from real helplessness before ever bringing anything to God.

The third year tithe keeps that same story moving forward in the present tense. A God who once had compassion on a homeless ancestor's family requires His now settled people to have the same compassion on the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow among them, refusing to let redemption become a private possession that stops circulating once it reaches the redeemed.

The chapter's closing title, treasured possession, becomes one of the story's clearest through lines. Spoken first at Sinai, repeated here, it is picked up centuries later and applied to the church in Christ, so the same love that singled out one landless, wandering family in the ancient world now singles out a people gathered "from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue," Revelation 7:9, still called God's own treasured possession.

And the mutual proclamation that ends the chapter, Israel declaring the LORD its God, the LORD declaring Israel His people, previews the deeper mutuality the gospel finally secures, not a covenant Israel must first perform correctly, but one sealed in Christ's own blood, where God's declaration over His people no longer waits on their worthiness. The chapter ends on the plains of Moab looking toward blessing and curse still to come, but the story it feeds runs on toward a people who will one day see His face and need no longer bring a confession, only praise.

quiz.q: How does the worshiper describe his ancestor in the firstfruits confession, verse 5?

options.text: 'My father was a wandering Aramean,' who went to Egypt few in number and became a great nation.
options.note: Verse 5 gives this exact confession.

options.text: 'My father was a great king who conquered many lands.'
options.note: The confession is one of humble beginnings, not conquest.

options.text: 'My father was born in the promised land.'
options.note: The confession specifically recalls Egypt and wandering, not the land.

options.text: No confession is recited at the firstfruits offering.
options.note: Verses 5-10 give the confession in full.

quiz.q: What does the worshiper do after reciting the confession and presenting the firstfruits basket?

options.text: Bow down before the LORD and rejoice in all the good things the LORD has given, along with the Levite and the foreigner.
options.note: Verses 10-11 describe this explicitly.

options.text: Immediately return home without any further act of worship.
options.note: The text explicitly describes bowing and rejoicing.

options.text: Burn the basket entirely as a whole offering.
options.note: The text describes the basket placed before the LORD and shared in rejoicing, not burned.

options.text: No further action is described.
options.note: Verses 10-11 describe explicit action.

quiz.q: Who receives the tithe in the third year, according to verse 12?

options.text: The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
options.note: Verse 12 names these four groups explicitly.

options.text: Only the king and his officials.
options.note: The text specifies the vulnerable, not royal officials.

options.text: Only the priests at the central sanctuary.
options.note: The text specifies a broader group including foreigners and the fatherless, not priests alone.

options.text: No recipients are named.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly names the recipients.

quiz.q: What title does the LORD give Israel in verse 18?

options.text: His treasured possession.
options.note: Verse 18 states this explicitly.

options.text: His hired servants.
options.note: The text uses the language of treasured possession, not hired service.

options.text: His distant relatives.
options.note: The text describes a close, chosen relationship, not mere distant kinship.

options.note: Verse 18 gives an explicit title.

quiz.q: What does verse 19 promise will happen if Israel keeps the covenant?

options.text: The LORD will set them high in praise, name, and honor above all the nations, and they will be a holy people to Him.
options.note: Verse 19 states this explicitly.

options.note: The text promises the opposite, honor above the nations.

questions: Israel's worship began with an honest confession of humble, even desperate, beginnings, 'a wandering Aramean.' How honest are you in recounting your own story of need before you turn to praise?
The firstfruits offering gave God the first and best before anything else was used. Where in your life are you giving God the leftovers rather than the first and best?
The third-year tithe was directed specifically to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow. Who are the vulnerable people in your own community that your generosity should be reaching?

Israel is called God's 'treasured possession,' a title the New Testament gives to the whole church in Christ. How does knowing you are personally treasured by God change how you see your own worth today?
This chapter ties genuine worship to reciting exactly what God has done. What specific things has God done in your own life that you need to recount and give Him thanks for today?

translationNotes.note: 'A wandering Aramean' most likely refers to Jacob, whose life and family were bound up with Aram-Naharaim; the phrase emphasizes precarious, landless beginnings before God's rescue.

This third-year tithe for the vulnerable may be the same tithe described in chapter 14 redirected in its third-year cycle, or a distinct additional provision; either way it establishes a structured, recurring provision for the poor within Israel's worship calendar.
'Treasured possession' translates segullah, a term used of a king's own private treasure, first applied to Israel at Sinai in Exodus 19:5 and later applied to the church in 1 Peter 2:9.
